calls.topic: Who You Are Now vs. Your Future Self
calls.recap: A pen-and-paper exercise mapping who you are today against the version of yourself you're working toward, and why that gap only closes when you start acting like her now instead of waiting for the right moment. Perfectionism came up as the biggest blocker in the room, along with the reminder that progress is measured by how fast you get back to baseline after a setback, not by never having one.

calls.topic: Mindset, Satiety, and Making Food Worth Eating
calls.recap: How the way you think about a meal changes the way your body responds to it, including the milkshake study where the same shake described as "indulgent" left people fuller than when it was described as "light." The practical half covered seasoning your food, plating it so it's actually appealing, prepping two proteins a week, and what does and doesn't need to be logged in Cronometer.

calls.topic: What Full Commitment Actually Looks Like
calls.recap: The expectations behind the program: check-ins done on time and in full, consistent progress photos, tracking weight and food, and leaning on your coaches instead of a social media algorithm for answers. Michelle also spoke openly about the gap between polarizing online content and how coaching actually works day to day, and made the case for 90/10 commitment over 80/20.

Rewriting vague goals as decisive "I will" statements, trading soft language (should, maybe, might, tried) for hard language, and treating FEAR as False Evidence Appearing Real. The through-line: the challenges don't get easier, you get stronger at handling them, so aim for 1% better rather than waiting until you can give 100%.

calls.topic: Precision Tracking and the Comparison Trap
calls.recap: Why logging honestly, especially on the days you'd rather not, is what builds the self-awareness that eventually makes intuitive eating possible, plus how whole single-ingredient foods behave differently in the body than processed ones at the same calorie count. The second half took on comparison: every plan here is individual, so the only comparison worth making is to your own past self.

calls.topic: Mindset, Confirmation Bias, and Training Fundamentals
calls.recap: Mindset as the thing driving every outcome, including how confirmation bias makes you find proof for whatever you already believe and how to reset a social media feed that's reinforcing the wrong one. The call also covered training basics: form before load, add reps before you add weight, and why a temporary drop in strength is normal rather than a sign you're going backward.

The introduction of the BIA Baddie Oath, the written set of standards behind the program: ownership over excuses, progress over perfection, consistency over intensity, fueling your body with respect instead of punishment, and training to become stronger rather than smaller. The group worked through which lines landed hardest, especially the shift from going to the gym to shrink to going to get strong.

January framed as the month of data, on the principle that a year is built by daily habits rather than by written goals, and that you can't manage what you don't measure. The group set goals across health, money, and career, then worked each one backward into the specific actions and tracking that would actually make it happen.

Getting through the holidays without absorbing everyone else's stress: how to walk into a hard conversation level-headed, set a boundary and actually hold it, and decompress afterward instead of letting it fester. One reframe stuck with the group all night, that these aren't tough conversations, they're necessary ones, and you control your reaction rather than the other person's emotions.

Reliability as a form of self-trust, keeping your word to yourself even when your mood says otherwise, and why coaching is really asking you for an identity shift. From there the call got practical about celebration season: portion control on the traditional dishes rather than macro-fying an entire holiday meal, handling alcohol-heavy gatherings, and finding ways to celebrate that aren't built around food.

calls.topic: Q4 Consistency, Sleep, and Circadian Rhythm
calls.recap: Holding your ground through Q4 instead of writing off the last three months of the year, then a deep dive on sleep: morning light, getting off blue light after dark, a cool and dark room, a consistent wind-down, and keeping naps to 15 to 30 minutes. Also covered was how to adapt your routine when a work or show schedule flips your entire day around.

Where your targets come from: how BMR and TDEE set your calorie range, why protein at roughly 0.8 to 1 gram per pound is about preserving muscle and staying full rather than bulking up, what carbohydrates actually do for energy and recovery, and why fats are non-negotiable for hormone health. The second half turned to emotional eating and how to recondition the habit of reaching for convenience food to manage a feeling.

What happens to partners, family, and friend groups when your habits change, and the sense of missing out that shows up around travel, restaurants, and gatherings. The nutrition half laid out a balanced philosophy: mostly whole foods with real room for treats, why "protein" on a package is often just marketing, and how to stay ingredient-aware without tipping into fear of food.

The beliefs about worth, money, food, and health you inherit without ever choosing them, and what it takes to be different rather than just do different. The group talked through growth mindset versus fixed mindset, advocating for yourself in a doctor's office, and the reminder that it is never too late to start.

calls.topic: Holding Your Goals in Social Situations
calls.recap: Standing firm on your goals when the room isn't set up for them: workplace food culture, peer pressure at gatherings, and drinking. The core skill the group kept returning to was getting comfortable saying no to an offer without needing to justify it, and setting boundaries around food that hold up even when you're not the one choosing the menu.

An unscripted call that turned into a conversation about what to do when someone questions your integrity, whether that's at work, in your family, or in a relationship. The answer the group kept circling: get clear on your own values first, take whatever the criticism can actually teach you, and then put the rest down instead of carrying it. It doubled as a reminder that being vulnerable isn't a weakness in how you lead or how you show up.

The group had a podcast as homework, Alex Hormozi's "15 brutally honest truths," and spent the call on the ones that hit hardest: pain is the price of progress, the hard way is the easy way, ignore the critics, and consistency beats talent. A long stretch on fear versus regret landed on doing the thing scared, and on practicing the part you're bad at instead of the part you're already good at. It closed on training questions, including why protein and hard training come before any supplement.

A goal-setting call built on the idea that saying a goal out loud turns it into a promise rather than a wish, anchored in the BIA equation: initiative plus action equals change. The practical thread ran in both directions on appetite, how to handle real hunger in a sculpt phase using high-volume, lower-calorie foods, and why a disappearing appetite is usually a stress response rather than a win. It closed on auditing your own time for what's genuinely a priority versus what's just filling space.

The call went after limiting beliefs, the quiet stories that cap your progress before the plan ever gets a chance. The big ones on the table: that you can outwork a bad diet, that cardio is required for fat loss, that age or pain rules out strength training, and that eating more food has to mean gaining weight. The coaches explained why calories often need to go up before a fat loss phase can work at all, and why sleep is the reset button everything else depends on.

calls.topic: What Are You Changing This Year?
calls.recap: A new-year goal-setting call with a sharper question attached: not just what you want this year, but what you're actually willing to change from last year to get it, and which obstacle you already know is coming. The conversation kept landing on the same blocker, getting in your own way by putting everyone else first, and on how much unspoken stress and over-responsibility end up showing up in your body.

calls.topic: Macros Are a Target, Not a Ceiling
calls.recap: The reframe of the night: your macros are a number to hit, not a cap to stay under, so coming in well below isn't a good day, it's a missed one. The group talked through what tracking is actually building toward, the knowledge to size up a plate without the scale later on, and where a food scale does and doesn't earn its place when you're eating out. It closed on holiday traditions and leaning into the parts of the season that were never really about the food.

A working session on the WOOP method, Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan, applied to goals heading into the holidays instead of waiting for January to start. The step most people skip is the second O, naming the obstacle you already know is coming so the plan exists before you need it, rather than becoming the reason things fell apart. It ties straight back to the equation the coaches keep returning to: initiative plus action equals change.

An honest conversation about what's still difficult even a year in: progress slow enough to make you want to quit, struggling to eat enough, and all-or-nothing thinking the moment you walk into a party. The practical takeaway was to arrive already fed and hydrated, because temptation does its best work when you show up hungry, and to treat frequency and portion as the real variables instead of banning foods outright.

A working session on protein: what to do when you're full long before you reach the target, why plant sources like edamame take real volume to count for as much as you'd think, and how much of what's marketed as "protein" is processed filler. Underneath it was the older advice a lot of the room was still unlearning, that you should eat as little as possible, skip the protein, and do more cardio.

A call deliberately pulled out of the fitness lane and pointed at what you actually want from your life, plus the action steps sitting between here and there. The group talked about naming dreams out loud, what to do when you genuinely can't name a passion right now, and why the do-or-die kind of passion isn't the only healthy version of it. The thread tying it back: the goals are reachable, but a fixed mindset about who you are will stop you long before the plan does.

A long conversation about the scale: why two pounds overnight is water, sleep, or your cycle rather than fat, and how many of us inherited our feelings about that number from the houses we grew up in. The group worked toward treating it as one piece of data alongside how clothes fit and how you feel. It also took the timeline question head on, that real change tends to show up around three months and takes closer to a year to fully believe.
